questions.prompt: A search box is bound with `Text="{Binding SearchText, Mode=TwoWay}"`, but the ViewModel only receives the text after the user tabs out of the box. What change gives live updates on every keystroke?
options: Change the mode to `Mode=OneWay`
Add `UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged`
Add `UpdateSourceTrigger=Explicit` to the binding
Change the mode to `Mode=OneTime`
questions.explanation: For `TextBox.Text` the default `UpdateSourceTrigger` is `LostFocus`, so the source updates on focus loss. `PropertyChanged` updates the source as soon as the text changes, for example for live search.

questions.prompt: In the demo window, a TextBox is bound TwoWay to `Name` (initially "Aman") and a Label shows `{Binding Name, Mode=OneTime}`. The user types "Rahul" into the TextBox. What does the Label show?
options: "Rahul", because `Name` raised `PropertyChanged` when it changed
Nothing, because OneTime bindings clear after the first read
"Aman", because a OneTime binding never updates after it is created
"AmanRahul", because OneTime bindings append each new value
questions.explanation: `OneTime` goes source → target once, when the binding is created; after that there are no updates, so the Label keeps the initial value even though `Name` changed.

questions.prompt: A ViewModel property changes in code, but a TextBlock bound to it with `Mode=OneWay` keeps showing the old value. What is the most likely cause?
options: The ViewModel does not raise `INotifyPropertyChanged` for that property
OneWay bindings only update when the window is resized or reloaded
The TextBlock needs `UpdateSourceTrigger=LostFocus` added to its binding
OneWay bindings never read the source again after startup
questions.explanation: Without `INotifyPropertyChanged`, the UI will not reflect changes from the ViewModel for OneWay or TwoWay bindings, so source properties must raise it.

questions.prompt: What does `[CallerMemberName]` do on the parameter of `OnPropertyChanged([CallerMemberName] string propName = null)`?
options: It makes `PropertyChanged` fire for every property on the class
It looks up the property name with reflection at runtime
It forces every caller to pass the property name as a string
The compiler fills in the calling property's name for you
questions.explanation: `[CallerMemberName]` automatically supplies the calling member's name to the parameter at compile time, which saves you from writing property names as strings like `"Name"`.

questions.prompt: Inside a ControlTemplate for Button, a Border needs the Background of the button using the template. Which binding does the lesson say is correct here?
options: `{Binding Background, ElementName=MyButton}`
`{Binding Background, RelativeSource={RelativeSource TemplatedParent}}`
`{Binding Background, RelativeSource={RelativeSource Self}}` on the Border
`{Binding Background}` with no source, using the DataContext
questions.explanation: `ElementName` only works within the same namescope and does not work well inside templates. Inside a ControlTemplate, `RelativeSource TemplatedParent` is the correct choice.

questions.prompt: A Delete button in a ListBox item template uses `Command="{Binding DataContext.DeleteUserCommand, RelativeSource={RelativeSource AncestorType=ListBox}}"` and `CommandParameter="{Binding}"`. Put what happens in order.
steps: The binding walks up the tree from the button
It reads that ListBox's `DataContext`, which is `MainViewModel`
Clicking the button executes `DeleteUserCommand`, receiving the current `User` as the parameter
questions.explanation: The item's own DataContext is a `User`, so the binding goes up to the ListBox, uses its `MainViewModel` DataContext to find `DeleteUserCommand`, and `CommandParameter="{Binding}"` passes the current `User`.
